tagline: A swing bridge leads into a village shaped by river trade.
intro: Route 82 crosses the Connecticut River on the East Haddam Bridge, reaching East Haddam beside the Goodspeed Opera House. The bridge itself is a designated scenic road. The scenic designation continues on the first 2.31 miles of Route 149, through the historic district along the Connecticut and Moodus rivers. The bridge combines a deck truss, a through truss and a swing span, with steel members joined by rivets.

The river landings had already lost commercial importance after the Civil War, when the railroad on the opposite bank became the principal freight connection. The crossing changed after a governor’s transportation commission recommended a bridge in 1909. Connecticut redirected ferry aid toward construction, making this one of the first bridges funded by the state. Work began in April 1912; the bridge opened on June 14, 1913. The road north had another identity in the 1920s: Highway 148, renumbered Route 149 in 1932.

Traveling east from Haddam, cross the three-span steel bridge into the village. At Route 149, Main Street leads north beside the Connecticut, then northeast along the Moodus River as East Haddam-Moodus Road. The historic district follows this road in a long line: the former Upper and Lower Landings grew together where steep ground to the east limited expansion.

moments.title: East Haddam Swing Bridge
moments.text: The East Haddam crossing makes room for two kinds of traffic: Route 82 above and river travel through its movable span. Alfred P. Boller designed the drawbridge to pivot, clearing a passage for vessels. Its three spans total 889 feet, including a 461-foot swing span. The opening on Flag Day in 1913 brought a speech by Governor Simeon E. Baldwin, a 17-gun salute and a Model-T parade. Below the riveted steel, stone-block piers and abutments rest on timber pilings. Special commissions oversaw construction because the State Highway Department then lacked authority over bridges.
moments.notice: Three steel spans cross the river; the swing span is 461 feet long.

moments.title: Goodspeed Opera House
moments.text: The theater at Goodspeed occupies the building’s top two floors. Scenery travels up from the dock area through a vacant shaft equipped with a winch. Merchant and banker William Henry Goodspeed built the venue in 1876–1877 for plays, despite its operatic name. After his death, its uses included a militia base, general store and transportation department storage. In 1959, citizens formed Goodspeed Musicals after the state condemned the building. The state agreed to sell it to the group for one dollar, on condition that they raise enough to restore and maintain it. Restoration led to its rededication in 1963.

moments.title: East Haddam Historic District
moments.text: Upper Landing and Lower Landing once traded with the East and West Indies. After the Civil War, their commercial importance declined as rail transport rose on the river’s west bank. The southern landing developed as a tourist destination and contains the bridge and village commercial district. The 110-acre historic district gathers buildings from both settlements along Route 149, including the town’s principal civic structures and Goodspeed Opera House. Its cemetery, park and monuments to Nathan Hale and General Joseph Spencer add other layers to the riverside village. The district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.
